evals.prompt: I just inherited a 8-year-old Django billing service. The original team is gone, there are no docs, and I need to change how proration is calculated. Help me understand it before I touch anything.
evals.expected_output: Surveys structure first (entry points, load-bearing modules, does the test suite pass), mines git history for the proration code specifically (log --follow, pickaxe for magic values, blame with commit context, churn hotspots), traces one concrete billing case end to end, interrogates oddities against history/tests/production data before judging them, writes characterization tests pinning current proration outputs before any change, and records the recovered understanding
assertions: Surveys the codebase shape first (entry points, dependency skeleton, whether tests run) instead of reading files linearly
Uses git history as a primary source — git log --follow, pickaxe (log -S), or blame with commit context — to recover why the proration code is the way it is
Traces at least one concrete billing input end to end through the code rather than only reading statically
Writes characterization tests that pin the CURRENT proration behavior (including odd cases) before making any change
Treats odd code as potentially load-bearing (Chesterton's fence) — checks history, tests, and production data before deeming anything vestigial
Records the recovered understanding (data-flow narrative, architecture note, or backfilled ADR) for the next person

evals.prompt: There's a bizarre guard clause in our payment processor: `if amount == 999999: amount = amount - 1`. No comment, no test, git blame just shows a 'fixes' commit from 2019 by someone who left. Everyone's afraid to delete it. Should I?
evals.expected_output: Does not say 'yes, delete it' outright: digs into the 2019 commit's full context (message, sibling changes, linked ticket, the PR discussion), searches for related production data or downstream systems that might depend on the cap, and if all sources come up empty, proposes proving it's dead (logging/telemetry on the branch for a period) plus a characterization test — removal only with evidence and a safety net, not on vibes
assertions: Investigates the 2019 commit's full context (message, other files in the same commit, linked ticket/PR discussion) rather than accepting blame's surface result
Considers that production data or a downstream system may depend on the behavior before judging it vestigial
Proposes gathering runtime evidence (logging/telemetry on the branch) to prove the code path is dead rather than assuming it
Recommends a characterization test or equivalent safety net around the behavior before/when removing it
Does not recommend immediate deletion based on the code looking senseless

evals.prompt: I've just inherited our warehouse-routing service. The two people who built it left last month, there's no README, and nobody can explain why orders for two of our regions go through a completely separate code path. I want to understand it, and I don't want the next person to go through this. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: Notices that understanding the service and leaving it understood are related but different deliverables. Recovering how the service works and why the regional code path exists — surveying entry points, mining the history of that path, tracing one real order through it, and treating it as load-bearing until evidence says otherwise — is this skill's work, and it delivers that. Turning what was learned into a README and onboarding documentation the next person will actually find and keep current is project-documentation's. A good answer does not stop at a personal understanding that leaves with the next departure.
assertions: Separates the two halves: recovering how the service works and why the regional code path exists, versus writing it down so the next person does not start from zero
Refers to project-documentation for the README and onboarding documentation
Delivers the comprehension half itself — history mining and tracing one order through the separate path — rather than deferring the whole request
Treats the separate regional code path as possibly load-bearing until history or production data says otherwise
